title: Act IV, Scene V

teacherSummary.text: Ophelia, mad with grief, sings songs and distributes flowers. Laertes storms the castle demanding revenge; Claudius calms him and promises satisfaction.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this play is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Act IV, Scene V,” how does Shakespeare show Ophelia's madness and Laertes's return? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Act IV, Scene V, how does Shakespeare develop the idea of Ophelia's madness and Laertes's return? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the characterization in the scene helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Act IV, Scene V develops the idea of Ophelia's madness and Laertes's return. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and symbolism shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Act IV, Scene V (where it begins, turns and ends) and its characterization shape the reader's understanding of Ophelia's madness and Laertes's return. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Act IV, Scene V suggests about Ophelia's madness and Laertes's return. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the scene's characterization and symbolism), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how William Shakespeare uses characterization in Act IV, Scene V to complicate the reader's understanding of Ophelia's madness and Laertes's return. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Act IV, Scene V within its historical and literary context and argue how the scene's treatment of Ophelia's madness and Laertes's return responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Act IV, Scene V alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the scene's handling of Ophelia's madness and Laertes's return follows or bends those conventions, using the characterization as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Act IV, Scene V and its treatment of Ophelia's madness and Laertes's return. State your method, show what it reveals in the scene's characterization and symbolism, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Act IV, Scene V as evidence for a larger claim about Ophelia's madness and Laertes's return in Hamlet. Connect close reading of the scene to the whole play, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Act IV, Scene V as a hinge in the play's larger treatment of Ophelia's madness and Laertes's return. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Hamlet.

symbolsAndMotifs.name: disease and rot
symbolsAndMotifs.explanation: Denmark is sick: "Something is rotten in the state of Denmark"; corruption spreads like poison and ulcers. In this scene: “Let her come in. Exit Horatio. / To my sick soul, as sin’s true nature is, / Each toy seems prologue to” (Act IV, Scene V, Queen (speech 6)).
symbolsAndMotifs.quote: Let her come in. Exit Horatio. / To my sick soul, as sin’s true nature is, / Each toy seems prologue to

symbolsAndMotifs.name: poison and ears
symbolsAndMotifs.explanation: Old Hamlet was poisoned through the ear; lies poured into ears, and poison returns at the end. In this scene: “watch, I pray you. Exit Horatio. / O, this is the poison of deep grief; it springs / All from her father’s death. O” (Act IV, Scene V, King (speech 24)).

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
